subject: Computer
q: The abacus, one of the earliest calculating devices, was first used in:
explanation: The abacus is the earliest known calculating device; it was used in China for counting and simple arithmetic.

subject: Computer
q: Napier's Bones, an early calculating tool made of rods, was invented by:
explanation: John Napier of Scotland invented Napier's Bones in 1617 for multiplication and division.

subject: Computer
q: The Pascaline, the first mechanical calculator, was invented in 1642 by:
explanation: Blaise Pascal built the Pascaline in 1642; it could add and subtract numbers with gears and wheels.

subject: Computer
q: The Stepped Reckoner, a calculator that could add, subtract, multiply and divide, was built by:
explanation: Leibniz built the Stepped Reckoner in 1673; it was the first calculator able to do all four basic operations.

subject: Computer
q: The Jacquard loom of 1804 used punched cards to control:
explanation: Joseph Jacquard's loom read holes punched in cards to weave patterns automatically; the idea later inspired computer punched cards.

subject: Computer
q: The Difference Engine, an early mechanical calculating machine, was designed in 1822 by:
explanation: Babbage designed the Difference Engine in 1822 to calculate mathematical tables automatically.

subject: Computer
q: Herman Hollerith's tabulating machine, which used punched cards, was first used in the census of:
explanation: Hollerith's punched-card machine counted the 1890 United States census far faster than counting by hand.

subject: Computer
q: The Harvard Mark I, one of the first large automatic computers, was completed in 1944 under:
explanation: Howard Aiken led the building of the Harvard Mark I, finished in 1944 with the help of IBM engineers.

subject: Computer
q: The Z3, the first working programmable computer, was built in 1941 by:
explanation: Konrad Zuse of Germany completed the Z3 in 1941; it was the first fully working programmable computer.

subject: Computer
q: ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic digital computer, was completed in 1946 at the:
explanation: ENIAC was built at the University of Pennsylvania by Eckert and Mauchly and switched on in 1946.

subject: Computer
q: UNIVAC I, the first computer made for business use, was delivered in:
explanation: UNIVAC I, delivered in 1951, was the first commercial computer; it was used by the US Census Bureau.

subject: Computer
q: EDSAC, the first computer to run a stored program in regular service, was built in 1949 at:
explanation: EDSAC at Cambridge ran its first program in May 1949 and was the first stored-program computer in regular use.

subject: Computer
q: The first generation of computers (1946-1959) was built using:
explanation: First-generation computers used vacuum tubes, which were large, hot and unreliable; ENIAC and UNIVAC I belong to this generation.

subject: Computer
q: The second generation of computers (1959-1965) was built using:
explanation: Second-generation computers replaced vacuum tubes with transistors, which were smaller, faster and used less power.

subject: Computer
q: The third generation of computers (1965-1971) was built using:
explanation: Third-generation computers used integrated circuits (ICs), many transistors packed on one small silicon chip.

subject: Computer
q: The fourth generation of computers (1971 onwards) was built using:
explanation: Fourth-generation computers use microprocessors, the whole CPU on a single chip, which made personal computers possible.

subject: Computer
q: The fifth generation of computers is based on:
explanation: Fifth-generation computers aim at artificial intelligence, using ULSI (ultra-large-scale integration) chips and parallel processing.

subject: Computer
q: Which of the following computers belongs to the first generation?
explanation: ENIAC, built with vacuum tubes in 1946, is a first-generation computer; IBM 1401 is second generation and IBM 360 is third.

subject: Computer
q: The IBM 1401, a famous business computer of the early 1960s, belongs to the:
explanation: The IBM 1401 used transistors, so it is a second-generation computer, widely used in business in the early 1960s.

subject: Computer
q: The IBM System/360, introduced in 1964, belongs to the:
explanation: The IBM System/360 used integrated circuits, which makes it a third-generation computer family.

subject: Computer
q: Machine language (binary code) was the main programming language of the:
explanation: First-generation computers were programmed in machine language, writing instructions directly in 0s and 1s.

subject: Computer
q: Assembly language became common in the:
explanation: Assembly language, which uses short codes like ADD and MOV instead of 0s and 1s, became common in the second generation.

subject: Computer
q: The CPU is called the brain of the computer because it:
options: Controls all operations and processes data
Connects the computer to the internet
explanation: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) carries out instructions and controls the whole computer, so it is called its brain.

subject: Computer
q: The ALU, a part of the CPU, is used to perform:
explanation: The Arithmetic Logic Unit performs calculations such as addition and subtraction and logical comparisons such as greater than or less than.

subject: Computer
q: The Control Unit (CU) of the CPU is responsible for:
options: Directing the flow of data and instructions
explanation: The Control Unit fetches instructions from memory, decodes them and tells the other parts of the computer what to do.

subject: Computer
q: The three main parts of a CPU are the ALU, the Control Unit and:
explanation: A CPU is made of the ALU, the Control Unit and registers, the tiny high-speed memory cells inside the processor.

subject: Computer
q: Registers are the fastest memory in a computer because they are located:
explanation: Registers sit inside the CPU, so the processor can reach them faster than RAM, cache or any other memory.

subject: Computer
q: The speed of a CPU is measured in:
explanation: CPU speed is the number of clock cycles per second, measured in hertz; modern CPUs run at several gigahertz (GHz).

subject: Computer
q: The basic working cycle of a CPU is:
explanation: The CPU fetches an instruction from memory, decodes what it means, and then executes it, repeating this cycle billions of times a second.

subject: Computer
q: The motherboard is the:
options: Chip that stores the operating system
Main circuit board connecting all parts of the computer
explanation: The motherboard is the large circuit board that holds the CPU, memory and other parts and lets them communicate with each other.

subject: Computer
q: A bus in a computer is a:
options: Pathway that carries data between parts
explanation: A bus is a set of wires that carries data and signals between the CPU, memory and input/output devices.

subject: Computer
q: BIOS, the program that starts a computer when it is switched on, is stored in:
explanation: BIOS (Basic Input Output System) is stored in ROM, so it is present even when the computer is switched off.

subject: Computer
q: POST, the self-test a computer runs when it is switched on, stands for:
explanation: POST checks the memory, keyboard and other hardware when the computer starts, before the operating system loads.

subject: Computer
q: The Intel 4004, released in 1971, was the world's first:
explanation: The Intel 4004 of 1971 was the first commercial microprocessor, putting a whole CPU on one small chip.

subject: Computer
q: The smallest unit of data in a computer is the:
explanation: A bit is a single 0 or 1, the smallest unit of data; all computer data is built from bits.

subject: Computer
q: A nibble is a group of:
explanation: A nibble is half a byte, made of 4 bits; two nibbles make one byte.

subject: Computer
q: One byte is equal to:
explanation: One byte is a group of 8 bits and can store one character, such as the letter A.

subject: Computer
q: How many bytes are there in one kilobyte (KB)?
explanation: One kilobyte equals 1024 bytes; computers use 1024 because they work in powers of 2.

subject: Computer
q: How many kilobytes make one megabyte (MB)?
explanation: One megabyte equals 1024 kilobytes, following the binary pattern of 1024 at every step.

subject: Computer
q: How many megabytes make one gigabyte (GB)?
explanation: One gigabyte equals 1024 megabytes; a typical movie file is about 1 to 2 GB in size.

subject: Computer
q: How many gigabytes make one terabyte (TB)?
explanation: One terabyte equals 1024 gigabytes; modern hard disks commonly hold 1 TB or more.

subject: Computer
q: RAM is called volatile memory because it:
options: Loses its data when the power is switched off
explanation: RAM (Random Access Memory) holds data only while the computer is on; everything in RAM is lost when the power goes off.

subject: Computer
q: ROM is called non-volatile memory because it:
options: Can hold only 1 KB of data
Is slower than a hard disk
Keeps its data even when the power is off
Loses its data when the power is off
explanation: ROM (Read Only Memory) keeps its data without power, which is why the startup program BIOS is stored in it.

subject: Computer
q: Cache memory is the fastest memory after registers, and it is placed:
options: Between the monitor and the keyboard
Between the CPU and the RAM
explanation: Cache memory sits between the CPU and RAM and stores copies of data the CPU uses again and again, so the CPU waits less.

subject: Computer
q: Primary memory of a computer consists of:
explanation: Primary memory is the memory the CPU can reach directly: RAM (temporary) and ROM (permanent).

subject: Computer
q: A hard disk stores data on:
explanation: A hard disk drive stores data magnetically on spinning metal platters; it keeps data even when the power is off.

subject: Computer
q: Compared with a hard disk drive (HDD), a solid-state drive (SSD) is:
options: Faster, because it has no moving parts
Slower, because it has no moving parts
explanation: An SSD stores data on flash memory chips with no moving parts, so it reads and writes much faster than a spinning hard disk.

subject: Computer
q: A standard CD can store about how much data?
explanation: A standard compact disc (CD) holds about 700 MB, enough for about 80 minutes of music or hundreds of documents.

subject: Computer
q: Which of the following is an input device?
explanation: A keyboard sends data into the computer, so it is an input device; a monitor, printer and speaker give out results.

subject: Computer
q: The longest key on a computer keyboard is the:
explanation: The spacebar is the longest key on the keyboard; it inserts a space between words.

subject: Computer
q: Most computer keyboards use the layout called:
explanation: The QWERTY layout, named after the first six letters of the top row, is the standard keyboard layout used worldwide.

subject: Computer
q: A scanner is an input device used to:
options: Copy pictures and documents into the computer
explanation: A scanner reads a paper document or photo and turns it into a digital image stored in the computer.

subject: Computer
q: MICR, used by banks to read cheques, stands for:
explanation: MICR reads the special magnetic-ink numbers printed at the bottom of bank cheques.

subject: Computer
q: OMR (Optical Mark Recognition) is used to read:
explanation: OMR scanners read the darkened bubbles on exam answer sheets, which is how objective tests are marked quickly.

subject: Computer
q: A barcode reader, commonly seen at shop counters, is a device that reads:
explanation: A barcode reader scans the black bars printed on a product and finds its price and details in the shop's computer.

subject: Computer
q: OCR technology is used to:
options: Convert printed text into editable digital text
explanation: OCR (Optical Character Recognition) reads printed or scanned text and turns it into text that can be edited on the computer.

subject: Computer
q: Which of the following is an output device?
explanation: A monitor shows the results of processing on the screen, so it is an output device; a keyboard, mouse and scanner are input devices.

subject: Computer
q: A laser printer prints using:
options: Toner powder and a laser beam
explanation: A laser printer uses a laser beam and fine toner powder; it prints fast and is common in offices.

subject: Computer
q: An inkjet printer prints by:
options: Spraying tiny drops of liquid ink on paper
Striking an inked ribbon with pins
Using a laser beam and toner
explanation: An inkjet printer sprays tiny droplets of ink onto the paper; it is cheap and prints good colour photos at home.

subject: Computer
q: A plotter is an output device used mainly to print:
options: Large drawings, maps and engineering plans
explanation: A plotter draws large-size output such as building plans, maps and charts, which a normal printer cannot handle.

subject: Computer
q: System software differs from application software because system software:
options: Is used only for typing letters
Manages the computer hardware and runs the system
explanation: System software, such as the operating system, controls the hardware; application software, such as Word, does a user's task.

subject: Computer
q: An operating system is a program that:
options: Manages hardware, files and programs of a computer
explanation: The operating system controls the processor, memory, files and devices, and lets the user run programs.

subject: Computer
q: File management, memory management and process management are functions of the:
explanation: The operating system manages files, memory and running programs, and controls the input and output devices.

subject: Computer
q: Linux is an example of a free and open-source:
explanation: Linux is a free, open-source operating system; its kernel was first written by Linus Torvalds in 1991.

subject: Computer
q: The Linux operating system kernel was first written in 1991 by:
explanation: Finnish student Linus Torvalds released the first Linux kernel in 1991; today Linux runs servers, phones and supercomputers.

subject: Computer
q: UNIX, one of the oldest operating systems, was developed in 1969 at:
explanation: UNIX was developed at Bell Laboratories in 1969 and became the base for many later systems, including Linux and macOS.

subject: Computer
q: MS-DOS, the early operating system of IBM personal computers, was released in 1981 by:
explanation: Microsoft supplied MS-DOS for the IBM PC in 1981; it was a text-based, single-user operating system.

subject: Computer
q: The first version of Microsoft Windows was released in:
explanation: Microsoft released Windows 1.0 in 1985, adding a graphical interface over MS-DOS.

subject: Computer
q: The graphical user interface (GUI) with windows, icons and a mouse was first made popular on personal computers by the:
explanation: The Apple Macintosh of 1984 made the GUI popular on personal computers, with icons, windows and a mouse pointer.

subject: Computer
q: A compiler is a program that translates:
options: One line of code at a time
The whole source program into machine code at once
explanation: A compiler converts the entire program into machine code before it runs; if there is an error, it reports all of them together.

subject: Computer
q: An interpreter differs from a compiler because it translates and runs a program:
explanation: An interpreter reads, translates and executes a program line by line, so an error stops it at the faulty line.

subject: Computer
q: An assembler is a translator program that converts:
explanation: An assembler converts low-level assembly language, written with short codes like ADD and MOV, into machine code.

subject: Computer
q: Machine language is the only language a computer understands directly, and it is written in:
explanation: Machine language uses only the binary digits 0 and 1; every other language must be translated into it before the computer can run it.

subject: Computer
q: FORTRAN, developed in 1957, was the first widely used:
explanation: FORTRAN (Formula Translation), developed by John Backus at IBM in 1957, was the first high-level language used for science and engineering.

subject: Computer
q: In binary, the number 1010 equals which decimal number?
explanation: Binary 1010 means 1x8 + 0x4 + 1x2 + 0x1 = 10 in decimal.

subject: Computer
q: The binary number 1111 equals which decimal number?
explanation: Binary 1111 means 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 in decimal.

subject: Computer
q: The binary number 100 equals which decimal number?
explanation: Binary 100 means 1x4 + 0x2 + 0x1 = 4 in decimal.

subject: Computer
q: ASCII is a 7-bit code that can represent how many different characters?
explanation: ASCII uses 7 bits, giving 2 to the power 7 = 128 characters, covering letters, digits and symbols.

subject: Computer
q: EBCDIC is an 8-bit character code that was mainly used by computers of:
explanation: EBCDIC is an 8-bit code developed by IBM for its mainframe computers.

subject: Computer
q: Unicode is a character code designed to represent:
options: Text in all the world's languages
explanation: Unicode can represent letters and symbols of nearly all the world's languages, unlike ASCII which covers mainly English.

subject: Computer
q: The hexadecimal number system has a base of:
explanation: Hexadecimal uses base 16, with digits 0-9 and letters A-F; it is used to write memory addresses and colours.

subject: Computer
q: The octal number system has a base of:
explanation: Octal uses base 8, with digits 0-7 only; it was used in early computer systems.

subject: Computer
q: A LAN (Local Area Network) connects computers in a:
options: Small area such as a room, office or building
explanation: A LAN links computers over a small area, such as one office or building, usually with high speed.

subject: Computer
q: A WAN (Wide Area Network) connects computers over a:
options: Large area such as cities, countries or the world
explanation: A WAN covers a large geographical area, such as cities or countries; the internet is the largest example of a WAN.

subject: Computer
q: A MAN (Metropolitan Area Network) is a network that covers a:
explanation: A MAN is bigger than a LAN and smaller than a WAN; it connects computers across a city.

subject: Computer
q: A modem is a device that:
options: Converts digital signals to analogue and back for the internet
explanation: A modem (modulator-demodulator) changes the computer's digital signals into analogue signals for a phone line, and back again.

subject: Computer
q: The World Wide Web (WWW) was invented in 1989 by:
explanation: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN in Switzerland.

subject: Computer
q: HTTP, used to open web pages, stands for:
explanation: HTTP is the set of rules browsers use to fetch web pages; HTTPS is the secure version of it.

subject: Computer
q: URL, the address of a web page, stands for:
explanation: A URL is the full address of a page or file on the internet, such as www.example.com.

subject: Computer
q: The first email was sent in 1971 by Ray Tomlinson, who chose which symbol to separate the username from the domain?
explanation: Ray Tomlinson sent the first email in 1971 and chose the @ symbol to separate the user's name from the computer's name.

subject: Computer
q: SMTP, the protocol used to send email, stands for:
explanation: SMTP is the standard protocol for sending email from one mail server to another; POP3 is used to receive it.

subject: Computer
q: Cloud storage means that data is stored on:
options: Only the computer's own hard disk
Remote servers on the internet, reached through a connection
explanation: In cloud storage, files are kept on servers on the internet, so they can be opened from any device; Google Drive and Dropbox are examples.

subject: Computer
q: The Brain virus, the first computer virus for personal computers, appeared in 1986 and was written in:
explanation: The Brain virus of 1986 was written in Lahore by the brothers Basit and Amjad Farooq Alvi; it infected the boot sector of floppy disks.

subject: Computer
q: Google, the world's most used search engine, was founded in:
explanation: Google was founded in 1998 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin while they were students at Stanford University.

subject: Computer
q: Microsoft Corporation was founded in 1975 by:
explanation: Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded Microsoft in 1975; its first product was a BASIC interpreter for the Altair computer.

subject: Computer
q: Apple Inc. was founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and:
explanation: Apple was founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne, who sold his share soon after.

subject: Computer
q: The first search engine on the internet was:
explanation: Archie, created in 1990, was the first search engine; it indexed files stored on FTP servers.

subject: Computer
q: A standard 3.5-inch floppy disk could store:
explanation: The common 3.5-inch floppy disk held 1.44 MB of data and was the usual way to move files in the 1990s.

subject: Computer
q: The CDC 6600, built in 1964 and regarded as the first supercomputer, was designed by:
explanation: The CDC 6600 of 1964, designed by Seymour Cray, is regarded as the first supercomputer.

subject: Computer
q: The Java programming language was created in 1995 by:
explanation: James Gosling and his team at Sun Microsystems created Java in 1995; it is widely used for Android apps and web systems.
